potaliputta.notes: MN 136 places the Buddha at the Bamboo Grove and Samiddhi in a wilderness hut. It is Samiddhi whom the wanderer visits there.

potaliya.notes: MN 54 calls Potaliya a gahapati and makes his objection to that title part of the conversation. AN 4.100 calls its speaker a paribbājaka and discusses praise and criticism. DPD cites both under its householder sense, but DPPN offers their identity as a conjecture. MN 53 is a neighboring citation.

pubbajira.notes: The village is at MN 144:13.5, one discourse beyond the mapped MN 143. The parallel at SN 35.87:13.5 reads pubbavijjanaṁ. Both texts say Channa had friendly families there. The exchange concerns Channa’s blamelessness and gives no support for the entry’s claim that the villagers were blamed for his death.

pubbavideha.notes: The packet misses pubbavidehānaṁ in the lists of continents at AN 3.80:4.2 and AN 10.29:2.2. Sujato translates it as lands east of Videha. DPD’s AN 3.81 reference is one discourse later in this edition.

pukkusa.notes: DN 16:4.26.1 identifies the Mallan disciple of Āḷāra Kālāma. Pukkusa 04 describes an occupational caste, attested in pukkusakule at AN 4.85 and pukkusakulā at MN 93. It belongs with the common-noun sense. AN 4.84 is a neighboring citation.

pukkusāti.notes: Both DPD lines point to the man in MN 140. Its kulaputta had already gone forth when he met the Buddha and died seeking a bowl and robes for ordination. MN 140:36.5 gives his destiny as a non-returner. The full DPPN entry also covers his liberation after rebirth in Aviha, where SN 1.50 and SN 2.24 name him. MN 139 and SN 1.49 are neighboring citations.

punabbasu.notes: His mother addresses the young yakkha in SN 10.7. SN 10.8 concerns Sudatta, and SN 10.12:14.3 is a chapter summary. MN 70 names the monks collectively as assajipunabbasukā. The candidate describes the child.

purāṇa.notes: MN 89:18.1 and SN 55.6:1.4 name Pasenadi’s two thapatis in the compound isidattapurāṇā. Migasālā names her father and uncle separately in AN 6.44 and AN 10.75. In the cited list at AN 6.120–139:1.12 the spelling is Pūraṇa, followed by Isidatta. AN 6.119 and AN 6.140 fall on either side of that list.

puṇḍarīka.notes: Despite the empty mention list, Snp 3.10:8.10 and AN 10.89:15.12 give twenty Uppalaka hells to one Puṇḍarīka. SN 6.10:6.10 has the short-i variant puṇḍariko nirayo. Sujato calls it the White Lotus hell.

puṇṇa.notes: MN 145 and SN 35.88 name Sunāparanta as Puṇṇa’s destination. Thag 1.70 is the second Puṇṇa’s verse, identified by both DPD and DPPN. Thag 1.4 names Mantāṇī as the first Puṇṇa’s mother. AN 1.196 is the named preacher within the grouped packet ID. Thig 1.3 and Thig 12.1 name nuns. For the ladle-holder, Ṭhānissaro reads puṇṇo dabbigāho at MN 93:18.71 as a person, as does DPPN. Sujato reads it as a ritual spoonful, which explains the missing packet mention. MN 94, MN 56, and the AN groups on either side of AN 1.196 are citation overlaps. In MN 57:2.1, acelo explicitly qualifies Seniya, while Puṇṇa is the Koliyan cow votary.

puṇṇikā.notes: MN 99:11.2 identifies Pokkharasāti’s bonded maid. In Thig 12.1 the water carrier is addressed as Puṇṇikā and the verse is attributed to Puṇṇā Therī. Neither passage connects the water carrier to Pokkharasāti. Only the woman in MN 99 has a candidate entry.

puṇṇiya.notes: Puṇṇiya asks his question in AN 8.82 and AN 10.83. AN 8.81 is a neighboring citation. AN 10.90:8.1 mentions him in the chapter summary.

pācīnavaṁsa.notes: SN 15.20:2.3 explicitly gives this former name of Mount Vepulla. The page reference also picks up SN 15.18 and SN 15.19.

pācīnavaṁsadāya.notes: AN 8.30 locates Anuruddha in this park among the Cetīs. MN 128 places him there with Nandiya and Kimbila, and Thag 2.18 names the park in Kimbila’s verse. MN 31 puts the same three men at Gosiṅga. The Meghiya episode in AN 9.3 and Ud 4.1 places the Buddha on Mount Cālikā and Meghiya’s mango grove by the Kimikāḷā. AN 8.8, AN 8.29, and MN 30 do not locate anyone at Pācīnavaṁsadāya.

pāricchattaka.notes: The packet misses the repeated pāricchattako koviḷāro from AN 7.69:1.1 onward, which Sujato calls the Shady Orchid Tree of the gods of the thirty-three. SN 48.68:1.1 spells it pārichattako. AN 7.68 is a neighboring citation.

pāvā.notes: MN 104 names Pāvā as the place where Nāṭaputta died. MN 103 is a neighboring citation. Ud 1.7:1.2 spells the shrine at Pāvā Ajakalāpaka, which the entry renders Ajakapālaka.

pāyāsi.notes: DN 23:32.3 already makes Uttara the organizer of Pāyāsi’s offering before he criticizes its quality. At 32.18 Pāyāsi authorizes better gifts. The entry describes Uttara as a recipient passed over and appointed afterward.

pāṭaligāma.notes: DN 16:1.28.7 connects the village with the future city Pāṭaliputta. The later city appears in AN 5.50, MN 52, MN 94, and SN 45.18. AN 5.49, MN 51, MN 95, and SN 45.15–17 are adjacent citations. The AN 11 parallel to MN 52 is AN 11.16, beyond the mapped AN 11.14–15. In Ud 8.6 the villagers offer lodging and the ministers Sunidha and Vassakāra serve the meal.

ragā.notes: The daughters appear by name in SN 4.25 and Snp 4.9. SN 4.24 tells of Māra’s own pursuit of the Buddha.

rakkhita.notes: MN 116:6.34 names an independently awakened Buddha. The available biography belongs to the elder named in the attribution of Thag 1.79.

rakkhitavanasaṇḍa.notes: Ud 4.5 locates the grove by its sal tree and the elephant’s attendance. In this account the Buddha seeks solitude because of the crowds at Kosambī. The entry also draws on the tradition about the monks’ dispute.

rammaka.notes: MN 26:2.5 names Rammaka as the brahmin whose hermitage the monks visit. MN 25 is a neighboring citation.
